'''''Pteridium aquilinum''''', commonly called '''[[bracken]]''', '''brake''', '''pasture brake, common bracken''', and also known as '''eagle fern''', is a species of [[fern]] occurring in temperate and subtropical regions in both hemispheres. Originally native to Eurasia and North America, the extreme lightness of its spores has led to it achieving a [[cosmopolitan distribution]].

== Description ==
Common bracken is a [[herbaceous]] [[perennial]] plant, [[deciduous]] in winter. The large, roughly triangular [[frond]]s are produced singly, arising upwards from an underground [[rhizome]], and grow to {{convert|0.3–1|m|ft|abbr=off|frac=2}} tall; the main stem, or stipe, is up to {{convert|1|cm|abbr=off|frac=2}} in diameter at the base. It dies back to ground level in autumn.<ref>Clapham, A.R., Tutin, T.G. and Warburg, E.F. 1968 ''Excursion Flora of the British Isles.'' Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|0-521-04656-4}}.</ref> The rhizome grows up to {{convert|3.5|m|ft|frac=2}} deep, about {{convert|5|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} in diameter, and up to {{convert|15|m|ft|round=5|abbr=on}} long. Because it regrows in the spring from an underground rhizome, ''P. aquilinum'' tends to be found in dense colonies of genetically identical fronds. Such colonies can be as much as 650 years of age, with individual rhizomes living up to 72 years.<ref>{{ cite journal | last= Page | first= C.N. | date= July 1976 | title= Taxonomy and Phytogeography of Bracken - A Review | journal= Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society of London |volume= 73 | issue= 1-3 | page= 28 }}</ref> One colony at Raakkyla, North Karelia, [[Finland]], studied by Eino Oinonen  proved to be {{cvt|489|m}} in diameter and based on growth rate, over 1400 years of age.<ref>{{cite journal | last= Oinonen | first= Eino | date= 1967 |title= The Correlation Between Size in Finnish Bracken....etc| journal= Acta Forestalia Finnica | volume= 83 | page= 41}}</ref>  In the spring as the plant enters its growing cycle, fiddleheads are first sent up from the rhizome. The density and area covered by a single rhizome maximizes that rhizome's chance of biological success when sending up new growth. The new growth presents as vertical stalks, coiled and covered in silver-grey hairs, that can be a metre or more in height before unfurling into fronds.<ref>{{Cite web |title=SCDNR - Species: Bracken Fern |url=https://www.dnr.sc.gov/marine/mrri/acechar/speciesgallery/Plants/BrackenFern/index.html |access-date=2022-06-04 |website=www.dnr.sc.gov}}</ref>

=== Reproduction ===
Sporangia are formed in sori on the underside of the frond.<ref name="Parnell">Parnell, J. and Curtis, T. 2012. ''Webb's An Irish Flora''. Cork University Press. {{ISBN|978-1-85918-478-3}}.</ref> They are arranged in narrow brown bands, and form spores over July, August and September.<ref name="common weeds">{{cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/commonweedsofuni00unit/page/8 |title=Common Weeds of the United States |date=January 1971 |publisher=Dover |isbn=0486205045 |location=New York |page=[https://archive.org/details/commonweedsofuni00unit/page/8 8]}}</ref>

== Taxonomy ==
It was traditionally treated as the sole species in the genus ''[[bracken|Pteridium]]'' (brackens); however, authorities have split and recognised up to 11 species in the genus. It was placed in the genus ''Pteridium'' by [[Friedrich Adalbert Maximilian Kuhn]] in 1879.<ref>
{{cite journal|author= Thomson, John A. | year= 2004|title=Towards a taxonomic revision of ''Pteridium'' (Dennstaedtiaceae). |journal=Telopea |volume=10 | issue=4|pages=793–803}}</ref> Genetic analysis of ''Pteridium'' from 100 different locations worldwide has revealed two distinct species and despite the common name "bracken" being shared, the "southern" species is ''Pteridium esculentum''. Though the southern ''P. esculentum'' shows little genetic diversity among physically isolated locations, ''P. aquilinum'' has distinct groups at the continental scale. However, evidence of long-distance gene flow was found in samples taken from Hawaii that presented elements of both North American and Asian subspecies of ''P. aquilinum.''<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wolf |first1=Paul G. |last2=Rowe |first2=Carol A. |last3=Kinosian |first3=Sylvia P. |last4=Der |first4=Joshua P. |last5=Lockhart |first5=Peter J. |last6=Shepherd |first6=Lara D. |last7=McLenachan |first7=Patricia A. |last8=Thomson |first8=John A. |date=October 2019 |title=Worldwide relationships in the fern genus Pteridium (bracken) based on nuclear genome markers |journal=American Journal of Botany |language=en |volume=106 |issue=10 |pages=1365–1376 |doi=10.1002/ajb2.1365 |issn=0002-9122 |pmc=6856829 |pmid=31545874}}</ref>

=== Etymology ===
Common bracken was first described as ''Pteris aquilina'' by [[Carl Linnaeus]], in Volume 2 of his ''[[Species Plantarum]]'' in 1753. The origin of the [[specific name (botany)|specific epithet]] derived from the [[Latin]] ''aquila'' "eagle". In the reprint of the ''Flora Suecica'' in 1755, Linnaeus explains that the name refers to the image of an eagle seen in the transverse section of the root.<ref>''radix oblique dissecta refert aliquatenus aquilam imperialem''</ref> In spite of this, the opinion has been forwarded that the name pertains to the shape of the mature fronds appearing akin to an eagle's wing.<ref name="floridaeth">{{cite book |last=Austin |first=Daniel F. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eS7lX_rC3GEC&q=Pteridium+aquilinum+eagle+wing&pg=PA551 |title=Florida ethnobotany |publisher=CRC Press |year=2004 |isbn=978-0-8493-2332-4 |page=551 |access-date=30 June 2010}}</ref> However, medieval scholars, including Erasmus, thought the pattern of the fibres seen in a transverse section of the stipe resembled a double-headed eagle or oak tree.

==Distribution and habitat==
Bracken is native to Europe, Eastern Asia and North America,<ref name="common weeds" /> but now has an almost [[cosmopolitan distribution]].<ref name="Baker-1974">{{cite journal |last=Baker |first=Herbert G |year=1974 |title=The Evolution of Weeds |journal=[[Annual Review of Ecology and Systematics]] |publisher=[[Annual Reviews (publisher)|Annual Reviews]] |volume=5 |issue=1 |pages=1–24 |doi=10.1146/annurev.es.05.110174.000245 |issn=0066-4162}}</ref> In the Americas, it is found throughout the continental [[United States]] and the [[Canada|Canadian]] provinces of [[Ontario]], [[Quebec]], and [[Newfoundland]]. Its range's northern border extends to southern [[Alaska]], while its southern reaches the northern portions of [[Mexico]], as well as the [[Greater Antilles]] in the [[Caribbean]].<ref name="common weeds" /> [[Weed]]y in acidic [[upland pasture]]s of [[northwestern Europe]].<ref name="Baker-1974" />

Bracken grows in pastures, deciduous and coniferous woodlands, and hillsides. It prefers [[acid]]ic soils.<ref name="common weeds"/>

An adaptable plant, bracken readily colonises disturbed areas. It can even be aggressive in countries where it is native, such as England, where it has invaded heather (''[[Calluna vulgaris]]'' (L.) Hull) stands on the North Yorkshire moors.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1111/j.1744-7348.1997.tb05399.x |title=The morphology of bracken (Pteridium aquilinum (L.) Kuhn) in the North York Moors—a comparison of the mature stand and the interface with heather (Calluna vulgaris (L.) Hull) 1. The fronds |journal=Annals of Applied Biology |volume=131 |pages=103–116 |year=1997 |last1=Whitehead |first1=S J |last2=Digby |first2=J }}</ref> In [[Ireland]], bracken is found in open woodland and sandy pastures.<ref name="Parnell"/>

== Toxicity ==
The plant contains the [[carcinogen]]ic compound [[ptaquiloside]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gomes |first1=Joana |last2=Magalhães |first2=Ana |last3=Michel |first3=Valérie |last4=Amado |first4=Inês F |last5=Aranha |first5=Paulo |last6=Ovesen |first6=Rikke G |last7=Hansen |first7=Hans C. B |last8=Gärtner |first8=Fátima |last9=Reis |first9=Celso A |last10=Touati |first10=Eliette |year=2012 |title=Pteridium aquilinum and Its Ptaquiloside Toxin Induce DNA Damage Response in Gastric Epithelial Cells, a Link with Gastric Carcinogenesis |journal=Toxicological Sciences |volume=126 |issue=1 |pages=60–71 |doi=10.1093/toxsci/kfr329 |pmid=22143989 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Ptaquiloside is known to cause haemorrhagic diseases in ruminants, tumours and haematological problems in non-ruminants, and is correlated with oesophageal and gastric cancer in humans.<ref name="Vetter 183–196" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hirono |first1=Iwao |last2=Ito |first2=Mitsuya |last3=Yagyu |first3=Shigeru |last4=Haga |first4=Masanobu |last5=Wakamatsu |first5=Kazumasa |last6=Kishikawa |first6=Teruaki |last7=Nishikawa |first7=Osamu |last8=Yamada |first8=Kiyoyuki |last9=Ojika |first9=Makoto |last10=Kigoshi |first10=Hideo |date=1993 |title=Reproduction of Progressive Retinal Degeneration (Bright Blindness) in Sheep by Administration of Ptaquiloside Contained in Bracken |url=https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jvms1991/55/6/55_6_979/_article |journal=Journal of Veterinary Medical Science |volume=55 |issue=6 |pages=979–983 |doi=10.1292/jvms.55.979 |pmid=8117827 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Chronic bracken consumption is also associated with upper digestive tract (UDT) squamous cell carcinomas in cattle (ruminants)—with the most aggressive and serious tumors located in the caudal (lower) UDT.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Masuda |first1=E.K. |last2=Kommers |first2=G.D. |last3=Martins |first3=T.B. |last4=Barros |first4=C.S.L. |last5=Piazer |first5=J.V.M. |date=2011 |title=Morphological Factors as Indicators of Malignancy of Squamous Cell Carcinomas in Cattle Exposed Naturally to Bracken Fern (Pteridium aquilinum) |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0021997510000770 |journal=Journal of Comparative Pathology |language=en |volume=144 |issue=1 |pages=48–54 |doi=10.1016/j.jcpa.2010.04.009 |pmid=20542519|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

High [[stomach cancer]] rates are found in [[Japan]] and [[North Wales]], where the young stems are used as a vegetable, but it is unknown whether bracken plays any part or if the cancer can be attributed to another cause.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=I A Evans |author2=B Widdop |author3=R S Jones |author4=G D Barber |author5=H Leach |author6=D L Jones |author7=R Mainwaring-Burton |name-list-style=amp |year=1971 |title=The possible human hazard of the naturally occurring bracken carcinogen |journal=Biochem. J. |volume=124 |issue=2 |pages=29P–30P |doi=10.1042/bj1240029pa |pmc=1177200 |pmid=5158492}}</ref> Consumption of ptaquiloside-contaminated milk is thought to contribute to human gastric cancer in the Andean states of [[Venezuela]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Alonso-Amelot |first1=Miguel E |last2=Avendaño |first2=Marisabel |year=2001 |title=Possible association between gastric cancer and bracken fern in Venezuela: An epidemiologic study |journal=International Journal of Cancer |volume=91 |issue=2 |pages=252–259 |doi=10.1002/1097-0215(200002)9999:9999<::AID-IJC1028>3.0.CO;2-H |pmid=11146454 |doi-access=free}}</ref> The [[spore]]s have also been implicated as carcinogens. Consumption of contaminated water and meat may be dangerous as well.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Tourchi-Roudsari |first=Motahhareh |date=2014 |title=Multiple effects of bracken fern under in vivo and in vitro conditions |journal=Asian Pacific Journal of Cancer Prevention |volume=15 |issue=18 |pages=7505–7513 |doi=10.7314/apjcp.2014.15.18.7505 |issn=2476-762X |pmid=25292020 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

However, ptaquiloside is water-soluble, and is reduced by soaking bracken in cool water.<ref name="Shaw" /> Korean and Japanese cooks have traditionally soaked the shoots in water and [[ash]] to detoxify the plant before eating.<ref name="pieroni" /> Ptaquiloside also degenerates at room temperature, which explains why the rat studies were done with the toxin stored at {{Convert|-20|C}}.<ref name="Shaw" /> At boiling temperature, the carcinogen denatures almost completely.<ref name="Shaw" /> [[Salt]] and [[Sodium bicarbonate|baking soda]] also help with volatilizing the chemical.<ref name="Shaw" />

It has been suggested that [[selenium]] supplementation can prevent as well as reverse the immunotoxic effects induced by ptaquiloside from ''Pteridium aquilinum''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Latorre |first1=A.O |last2=Caniceiro |first2=B.D |last3=Wysocki |first3=H.L |last4=Haraguchi |first4=M |last5=Gardner |first5=D.R |last6=Górniak |first6=S.L |year=2011 |title=Selenium reverses Pteridium aquilinum-induced immunotoxic effects |journal=Food and Chemical Toxicology |volume=49 |issue=2 |pages=464–470 |doi=10.1016/j.fct.2010.11.026 |pmid=21112370 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Uses ==

=== Food ===
[[File:Warabi_mochi_1.jpg|thumb|Commercially packaged ''warabimochi'' (bracken jelly) in Japan]]

Despite its established toxicity, ''P. aquilinum''{{'}}s global distribution—it is the fifth most widely distributed common weed species in the world—means that it has a long history of being consumed in many parts of the world.<ref name="Vetter 183–196">{{Cite journal |last=Vetter |first=János |date=2009-03-03 |title=A biological hazard of our age: Bracken fern [ Pteridium aquilinum (L.) Kuhn] — A Review |url=https://akjournals.com/view/journals/004/57/1/article-p183.xml |journal=Acta Veterinaria Hungarica |language=en |volume=57 |issue=1 |pages=183–196 |doi=10.1556/avet.57.2009.1.18 |pmid=19457786 |issn=1588-2705|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The toxicity and wide distribution has led to variation in cultural attitudes towards the consumption of the plant. In the United Kingdom where ''P. aquilinum'' is extremely successful, the rhizome was once consumed during and after World War I.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Marrs |first1=R. H. |last2=Watt |first2=A. S. |date=November 2006 |title=Biological Flora of the British Isles: Pteridium aquilinum (L.) Kuhn |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1365-2745.2006.01177.x |journal=Journal of Ecology |language=en |volume=94 |issue=6 |pages=1272–1321 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2745.2006.01177.x |bibcode=2006JEcol..94.1272M |s2cid=85114338 |issn=0022-0477|url-access=subscription }}</ref> However the Royal Horticultural Society now explicitly advises against its consumption due to toxicity.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bracken / RHS Gardening |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/weeds/bracken |access-date=2022-06-04 |website=www.rhs.org.uk |language=en-gb}}</ref>

Bracken is a widely eaten [[vegetable]] in Korea, Japan, the [[Russian Far East]], and parts of China, where it has historically been one of the most important wild vegetables consumed.<ref name="Shaw">{{Cite news|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/health/archive/2011/06/the-bracken-fern-a-natural-born-killer/241271/|title=The Bracken Fern: A Natural Born Killer?|last=Shaw|first=Hank|date=30 June 2011|work=[[The Atlantic]]|access-date=19 April 2017}}</ref> Populations of these countries where bracken is traditionally consumed have been able to access bracken in new locations after immigrating due to ''P. aquilinum''{{'}}s global ubiquity.

In Korea, bracken is known as ''gosari''. It is soaked, parboiled, and stir-fried, and often eaten as a side dish (''[[namul]]'').<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/02/16/dining/cafe-lily-review-bensonhurst-korean-uzbek.html|title=At Cafe Lily, the Korean-Uzbek Menu Evokes a Past Exodus|last=Mishan|first=Ligaya|date=16 February 2017|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=19 April 2017}}</ref> It is also a classic ingredient of [[bibimbap]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://isthmus.com/food-drink/reviews/five-star-korean-bbq/|title=I brake for fernbrake|last=Fontella|first=Amelia Cook|date=16 February 2017|work=[[Isthmus (newspaper)|Isthmus]]|access-date=19 April 2017}}</ref>

In Japan, bracken is known as ''warabi'' (蕨, ワラビ), and a jelly-like starch made from it is a key ingredient for the chilled dessert ''[[warabimochi]]''.  As a type of ''[[sansai]]'' (mountain vegetables), young bracken shoots are steamed, boiled, or cooked in soups. The shoots are also preserved in salt, [[sake]], or [[miso]].<ref name="pieroni">{{cite book |editor1-last=Prance |editor1-first=Ghillean |editor2-last=Nesbitt |editor2-first=Mark |last1=Pieroni |first1=Andrea |author-link=Andrea Pieroni (ethnobotanist) |date=2005 |title=The Cultural History of Plants |publisher=Routledge |page=35 |isbn=0415927463}}</ref>

[[Ohlone people]] of California, who called the plant ''witt'' or by the name adopted from [[Californios]] ''manita'', ate the young fronds of the ''pubescens'' variety raw or cooked. They also used the plant medicinally and in crafts.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Bocek|first=Barbara R.|date=1984|title=Ethnobotany of Costanoan Indians, California, Based on Collections by John P. Harrington|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/4254616|journal=Economic Botany|volume=38|issue=2|pages=247|issn=0013-0001}}</ref>

Bracken shoots have been used to produce beer in [[Siberia]], and among indigenous peoples of North America.<ref name="pieroni"/>

The [[rhizome]] can be ground into flour to make bread. In the [[Canary Islands]], the rhizome was historically used to make a [[porridge]] called ''gofio''.<ref name="pieroni"/>

Bracken leaves are used in the [[Mediterranean]] region to filter sheep's milk, and to store freshly made [[ricotta]] cheese.<ref name="pieroni"/>

The word Nooksack means "always bracken fern place" in the [[Nooksack language]], and the rhizome of the plant was eaten extensively by the Nooksack people and other tribes of the Pacific Northwest.<ref>{{cite web |title=Nooksack Tribe Website |url=https://nooksacktribe.org/about/ |website=nooksacktribe.org/about/ |access-date=21 January 2026}}</ref>

Young fronds of the bracken can be harvested easily and should be cooked for 30 to 60 minutes. Mature bracken is toxic due to thiaminase and can be destroyed by cooking. Should be avoided if not skilled enough to prepare it.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hall |first=Alan |title=The Wild Food Trailguide |date=1973 |publisher=Holt, Rinehart, Winston |isbn=0-03-007701-X |location=Canada |publication-date=1973 |pages=33 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Pharmacology ===
''P. aquilinum'' has been investigated for its anti-inflammatory and antioxidative properties.<ref>{{cite journal |pmid=25973486 |year=2015 |last1=Dion |first1=C |title=Evaluation of the anti-inflammatory and antioxidative potential of four fern species from China intended for use as food supplements |journal=Natural Product Communications |volume=10 |issue=4 |pages=597–603 |last2=Haug |first2=C |last3=Guan |first3=H |last4=Ripoll |first4=C |last5=Spiteller |first5=P |last6=Coussaert |first6=A |last7=Boulet |first7=E |last8=Schmidt |first8=D |last9=Wei |first9=J |last10=Zhou |first10=Y |last11=Lamottke |first11=K |doi=10.1177/1934578X1501000416 |s2cid=8419285 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

=== Traditional medicine ===
In Finnish traditional medicine, bracken has been used as a remedy in many ways:<ref name="Piirainen">{{cite book |last1=Piirainen |first1=Mikko |title=Kotimaan luonnonkasvit |last2=Piirainen |first2=Pirkko |last3=Vainio |first3=Hannele |date=1999 |publisher=WSOY |isbn=951-0-23001-4 |location=Porvoo, Finland |page=499 |language=fi |trans-title=Native wild plants}}</ref>
* [[Elias Lönnrot]] advised to use a powder made of the plant's roots to drive away maggots. 
* A [[decoction]] made of bracken was used to treat stomach problems, [[gout]] and joint pain.
* The leaves have been used as filling in mattresses, because it was believed to lessen rheumatic pain and drive away [[vermin]].
In California, Ohlone people traditionally used the roots in a decoction as a hair rinse or in a paste which was rubbed in the scalp to encourage hair growth.<ref name=":0" />

=== Crafts ===
Ohlone people used the fronds extensively as umbrellas, for roofing their homes, and to line acorn-leaching pits and earth ovens. They also used the roots in basketry.<ref name=":0" />
